client: I've been really struggling lately because I failed two exams this semester and now I can't stop thinking about whether I'll even be able to graduate on time. The anxiety is just constant — like, it's there when I wake up, it follows me to class, and it keeps me up at night. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the problem is real — those grades are already there and I can't undo them.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds genuinely exhausting — the worry following you from morning to night, and yet your voice tells me there's also a kind of quiet resignation underneath it, like you've already started to brace for the worst. You're absolutely right that those grades can't be erased, but the story you're telling yourself *about* what they mean for your future — that's something we can look at together, because our minds often jump to the most catastrophic conclusion when we're this depleted. Would you be willing to explore what graduating "on time" actually means to you, and whether there might be more paths forward than the anxiety is currently letting you see?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: I mean, I hear what you're saying, but honestly, "more paths forward" feels kind of hollow right now, because every path I can think of still has this giant obstacle in the way. Like, my parents have this very specific picture of what my life is supposed to look like, and graduating late or switching programs isn't just disappointing to them — it feels like a complete failure of who I'm supposed to be. I'm willing to talk about it, I guess, but I'm not sure exploring it is going to change the actual reality of the situation.
therapist: The way you're speaking — fast, tense, pitched high — tells me this isn't abstract worry for you, it's something that feels urgent and pressing right in this moment, like you're almost racing against the anxiety itself. What strikes me is that you're not just afraid of failing exams — you're afraid of failing *as a person*, specifically in the eyes of people whose love might feel conditional on you hitting certain milestones. That belief — that your worth is tied to a very specific life script — is exactly the kind of thought pattern that CBT can help us examine, not to dismiss the real pressure you're under, but to ask: *is that actually true*, and who decided that script in the first place?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... yeah, you're probably right that it goes deeper than just the exams themselves, but when you say "who decided that script" it almost sounds too simple, like I can just trace it back to one moment and suddenly it loses its power. My parents never sat me down and said "your worth depends on your grades" — it was just always in the air, in every conversation about the future, in the way they lit up when I did well and got quiet when I didn't. So even if I intellectually know the belief might not be "true," I don't know how to make that land somewhere that actually changes how I feel when I'm staring at a syllabus at midnight.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but very fast, like the words are tumbling out under pressure — tells me this insight is landing somewhere real and tender, even as you're pushing back on it. You've just described something really important: this belief wasn't taught in a single lesson, it was *absorbed* through a thousand small moments, which actually makes it harder to dislodge intellectually but also means we don't need one magical "aha" to undo it. The goal isn't to think your way out of the feeling in one conversation — it's to slowly build enough evidence from your own life that a different story starts to feel just as true as the one you inherited.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually does feel that — like something got poked that I usually keep pretty covered up. But I guess my worry is, what evidence? Because when I look at my actual life right now, I mostly just see proof that the old story is right — I do end up alone, people do drift away, so where am I supposed to find this counter-evidence you're talking about?
therapist: The way you're speaking — very fast, pitched high, like something urgent is pressing up through you — tells me that what just came out went somewhere deeper than the exams, and I want to gently stay with that: you moved from grades to "I end up alone," and that shift matters enormously. I want to ask you something carefully — when you say people drift away, are you interpreting their distance as *evidence about your worth*, or could there be other explanations you haven't been allowed to consider? Because a mind in pain is a very selective collector of evidence — it holds onto every piece that confirms the old story and quietly discards the rest.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to agree with it, because it sounds logical. But when I actually try to think of other explanations for why people drift away, my mind just... goes blank, and then circles back to "well, maybe it really is me." It's not like I'm choosing to collect the bad evidence — it just feels like that IS all the evidence there is.
therapist: Your voice carries something quieter and heavier now — like you've said something that feels very true and very lonely at the same time, and I want to sit with that for a moment rather than rush past it. What you're describing — the mind going blank and then defaulting to "it must be me" — isn't a sign that the evidence is real; it's actually a hallmark of how depression and anxiety work, they don't just make us feel bad, they literally narrow our thinking so that alternative explanations become genuinely hard to access. So the blankness itself isn't proof — it's a symptom, and that's something we can very gently start to work with together.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... that the blankness is just a symptom and not some kind of truth my brain already knows. But it's hard, because in the moment it doesn't feel like a symptom, it feels like clarity, like I'm finally seeing things as they really are. And then I worry that even if I try to look for other explanations, I'm just going to be making excuses for myself, lying to myself almost.
therapist: Your voice is fast and pitched high even as the words themselves feel almost resigned — like part of you is working very hard to hold something together while also quietly believing it might already be broken. What you just named is one of the most painful traps depression sets: it disguises itself as clarity, as finally seeing the truth, so that the most distorted thinking feels like the most honest thinking. Searching for other explanations isn't lying to yourself — it's actually the braver, harder thing, because it means challenging a story that feels certain, and that takes real courage, not self-deception.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me actually wants to believe that, but... it's hard not to feel like you're just doing your job, you know, giving me the hopeful reframe because that's what therapists are supposed to do. Like, what if in my case the "distorted thinking" actually is just accurate thinking, and I'm the one person where the pessimistic read is the correct one? I've been alone for so long that it doesn't feel like a depression story anymore, it just feels like my life.
therapist: The fact that you're questioning whether I'm being genuine — that's not resistance, that's actually you protecting yourself, and it makes complete sense given how long you've had to rely only on yourself. I want to be honest with you: I can't prove to you in this moment that your thinking is distorted, and I'm not going to pretend the pain of long loneliness is just a cognitive error to be reframed away. What I will say is that "this has been true for a long time" and "this will always be true" are two very different statements, and your mind — very fast, very pressured right now, even as your voice stays soft — is quietly collapsing them into one.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: That distinction you're making... I hear it, and part of me wants to hold onto it, but another part of me is already looking for the catch. Like, okay, "has been" versus "will always be" — that sounds logical, but when you're lying in bed at midnight and your phone hasn't made a sound in three days, logic doesn't really show up to help. I guess what I'm asking is, what do I actually do with that difference when I'm in the middle of it and it just feels like evidence?
therapist: Your voice is soft but moving fast, like you're reaching for something real and practical this time — not just comfort, but an actual tool — and I want to honor that. When you're at midnight and the phone is silent, the goal isn't to out-logic the pain; it's to do one tiny, concrete thing that interrupts the spiral just long enough to create a small gap — texting one person something low-stakes, getting up and making something warm, writing down the thought "this is evidence I'm alone forever" and next to it writing "or it's a Tuesday night." That gap won't fix everything, but it's how the distinction between "has been" and "will always be" stops being a therapy concept and starts becoming something you can actually touch.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I like the "or it's a Tuesday night" thing — that actually made me almost smile, which is weird because nothing feels funny right now. But I guess my worry is that in the moment, when it's actually midnight and I'm actually spiraling, I won't remember any of this. It'll just feel like proof again, not like a Tuesday.
therapist: That almost-smile matters more than you might think — it's a tiny crack of light, and your voice right now is softer and a little more settled than it's been, like something in you is cautiously breathing out. Your worry about forgetting is completely valid, which is exactly why we don't leave it to memory — you write "or it's a Tuesday night" on your phone, your mirror, somewhere it exists outside your mind so it can show up even when your mind won't. You don't have to remember the whole conversation, you just need one small thing waiting for you in the dark.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of writing it somewhere... but I'm already thinking about how I'll probably just scroll past it on my phone without really seeing it, you know? Like, my brain has this way of making familiar things invisible, especially when I'm in that dark place and not really looking for help anyway. I guess I'm just not sure if a note is enough to cut through that kind of fog.
therapist: Your voice is soft and fast but pitched very high, like you're thinking out loud while also bracing for disappointment — and what you're describing, the way familiar things become invisible in the fog, is real and worth taking seriously rather than just problem-solving around. So instead of one easy-to-scroll-past note, let's think about something with more friction — a physical sticky note on your water bottle, an alarm titled "or it's a Tuesday night" set for 11pm, something that meets you in your body and your routine rather than competing with a screen. The goal isn't a perfect system — it's just making it slightly harder for the fog to win completely.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
